title: The Factors That Affect Learning - intro
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Opening the second half of the series, Skelton argues that teaching is not a clean science but a daily improvisation. He builds a vivid composite morning around a student called Carrie and her teacher, showing the dozens of uncontrolled variables, from moods to broken internet to parent meetings, that undermine any tidy hypothesis. The profession's nervousness about this chaos, he suggests, drives teachers to cling to gurus, fads like Brain Gym, and fixed commitments that seem to hold variables still. His remedy is to keep learning itself as the constant, the hedgehog concept. He then explains that his twelve factors come from decades of visiting hundreds of schools and from the wider research, and he concedes that no single magic ingredient exists.
points: Clean-cut scientific models of teaching are a dangerous illusion favoured by outsiders, because real classrooms are fuzzy and full of uncontrolled variables.
Professional insecurity pushes schools toward unevidenced fads and gurus that offer a feeling of control.
Holding learning as the constant gives everyone a common focus that survives the daily chaos.
The factors he will cover come from close observation of schools plus research, and he admits that we know less than we like to claim.
quotes: Whatever learning and teaching are, they aren’t pure sciences, even though on their best days they occasionally share some of science's characteristics. Most daily teaching is based on a hypothesis or a number of hypotheses.

The ‘scientific, clean-cut’ version of what is happening while learning and teaching is taking place is a dangerous illusion. It is beloved by so many people outside the classroom because they need to believe it to devise their policies and make their criticisms.

Given all of this, learning and teaching can feel much more like being at a comedy club on improv night. There are a small number of known themes, the audience is at least as in control of the atmosphere as the comedian and the club set-up will range from hopeless to helpful.

One important - and paradoxical - outcome of the profession’s nervousness is that we are always looking for solutions that seem as though they might hold at least some of the variables steady for a while. This is why teachers and schools develop commitments to particular factors that affect learning whether they are valid or not.

That’s why some teachers’ conversations continually reference the latest guru, the latest course and the newest TedTalk as though - at last - their problems have finally been solved or, at least, the variables have been reduced. It has always been like this.

Disappointingly, but unsurprisingly, we have discovered no one single magic thing other than that the best schools have a relentless commitment to learning - to getting better - as their hedgehog concept, the single idea that drives everything else they do. But, over time, we have been able to identify a number of elements that are implemented differently in better schools than they are in less effective schools.

This is another reason why having learning as a Hedgehog Concept matters so much. It provides a common focus - a real commitment - for everyone, for Carrie and her fellow students, for the teacher and her colleague, for the leadership of the school, for parents and others that transcends all these variables.
